title: HTTP, browser caching, and the real network path
outcome: Separate HTTP caching, application state, CORS, cookies, and request success.
useCase: Stale dashboards and cross-origin application debugging.
benefits: Finds the actual boundary instead of adding random cache flags.
drawbacks: Several caches and identity rules can interact.
version: Modern JavaScript / TypeScript · Vue 3.5 where applicable · browser APIs
cue: Name the layer before changing the setting.

trace.title: Browser request
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

fetch resolves for an HTTP 404 or 500. Check response.ok before treating the body as success.

A network failure is different from a server returning a deliberate error response.

The browser HTTP cache, a service worker, your query cache, and the server cache are separate copies. Cache-Control describes HTTP caching policy.

An ETag can let the server say “not changed.” A fresh fetch call does not prove the server recomputed the data.

Cookies are sent according to origin/site, credentials mode, SameSite, and cookie attributes. CORS is a browser response-access rule, not authorization.

A preflight request checks whether the browser may send a certain cross-origin request. Inspect both request and response headers before changing settings.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Trace DNS → connection/TLS → request headers → server response → HTTP cache → app adapter → UI state. When the page is stale, identify which layer supplied the stale copy.

A 304 response is used with a cached representation. A 200 with old data can come from a backend cache.

A CORS error may hide a response from JavaScript while the server still received the request. Do not assume a browser error means no side effect happened.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail: Returning Access-Control-Allow-Origin:* does not make cookie-based cross-origin requests universally work. Sending a retry after a hidden response can repeat a server write.
